entry.title: Oura is going public, but these smart ring companies are coming for its crown
entry.body: The smart ring market is getting crowded, and Oura isn’t waiting around to see what happens next: it officially filed to go public on September 3. The company is killing it right now. The Finnish outfit’s revenue nearly doubled to $1.21 billion for the nine months ended June 30. Oura said it sold 3.6 million rings over the past year, and that it has around 5 million paid members. The company’s move to go public follows the recent launch of the Oura Ring 5, its slimmest and lightest ring yet. But while Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals are emerging from all corners to dethrone it, each betting on a different angle. For example, French company Circular announced this week that its upcoming ring will allow users to tap to pay with their ring, while Chinese company RingConn debuted a ring this year that added haptic vibrations. Indian company Ultrahuman separately announced this week that it raised $70 million with backing from Qualcomm’s venture arm as it looks to build a ring that it says will be able to run software directly on the device and eventually power everything from AI interactions to games. The race to beat Oura isn’t just about enhanced health and sleep tracking anymore. It’s now about seeing which company can cram the most smartphone-like features into a two-gram titanium band before someone ends up shipping a ring that lets you doomscroll TikTok or answer calls or do your taxes. I mean, we’re already seeing smart rings with screens, like the Pebble Halo, although it’s currently only available in India, as well as rings that promise touchpads, like the Dreame Ring. The irony is that the initial appeal with smart rings was that they made technology and health tracking feel less intrusive than devices like smartwatches and smartphones, given you can step away from a screen while still keeping tabs on your health. With the way things are headed in the smart ring industry, though, we may just end up slipping mini smartphones on our fingers. All of this is to say that the smart ring market is getting increasingly confusing, so we’ve rounded up the most notable contenders vying for Oura’s crown. Ultrahuman Earlier this year, Ultrahuman unveiled its third-generation smart ring, the $479 Ring Pro, which is set to begin shipping in the U.S. business was disrupted in October 2025 after the U.S. International Trade Commission ruled in Oura’s favor in a patent dispute. The ruling prevented the company from importing new ring inventory into the country, so Ultrahuman developed the Ring Pro with a redesigned form factor in order to circumvent Oura’s patent. The Ring Pro features a redesigned heart-rate sensing system aimed at improving signal quality during sleep, along with a new dual-core processor that enables more accurate data collection and greater on-device processing. As noted earlier, Ultrahuman looks to be more ambitious with future rings as it aims to go beyond sleep and health tracking. Circular Circular’s upcoming Ring 3 series, which consists of a Pro model and a Slim option, is expected to launch early next year. Both of the smart rings will feature an integrated NFC chip for contactless payments and on-finger vibrations that can be used for silent wake-up alarms, reminders, vital health alerts, and more. The Ring 3 Pro features a slimmer design than its predecessor and comes with FDA-cleared ECG for AFib detection, blood pressure trend tracking, glucose tracking, advanced sleep analysis, and comprehensive biometric monitoring. Pricing for the upcoming rings is not yet available. RingConn The RingConn Gen 3, which launched in May and starts at $349, features vascular health insights that use sensor data from the ring to assess changes in vascular strain over time after calibration with externally measured blood pressure values. It also tracks heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, sleep, activity, and stress, among other metrics. Additionally, it features vibration alerts for health changes, sedentary reminders, and low battery. Unlike Circular, which leans on haptics to make its ring more communicative, RingConn mostly sticks to vibration as a health-alert mechanism. Samsung Samsung became the first major tech giant to launch a smart ring in 2024. The Galaxy Ring, which costs $399, is arguably the strongest contender for anyone already invested in Samsung’s ecosystem of devices. Compared with other smart rings on the market, the Galaxy Ring is relatively basic when it comes to advanced health and sleep tracking. It lacks features such as sleep apnea detection, which are offered by RingConn, Oura, and Ultrahuman, as well as AFib detection, which is available on Circular and RingConn smart rings. Dreame Dreame, a relatively new entrant to the smart ring market, unveiled a ring earlier this year with haptic alerts for alarms, calls, messages, and more, along with a small touchpad that lets you do things like skip a song or snap a photo on your phone. It’s also said to offer heart rate tracking, blood oxygen monitoring, heart rate variability insights, sleep analysis, and more. Pricing and availability have yet to be announced.
entry.summary: While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, a growing number of rivals are now racing to dethrone it by trying all sorts of approaches to get an edge over it.

entry.title: There May Not Be an iPhone 18 This Year - WIRED
entry.body: Every year around this time, Apple announces new iPhones. The products go on sale soon after, usually ranging from a base model to more premium and more expensive Pro models. But this year will likely be different—not just because the company has a brand-new CEO. Apple’s iPhone event will be held on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern), announced last week with the title “Surprise and Shine!” If you tune into the livestream, expect the announcement of an iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and, if all the rumors and widely held analyst expectations are true, the first look at an Apple foldable device. Based on leaks and the ongoing tech rumor mill and its decent track record for figuring these things out, Apple is expected to prioritize its more expensive, premium devices this year and hold off on announcing its base model iPhone 18. That cheaper model is rumored to launch in the spring of 2027, potentially alongside an iPhone 18e and maybe a second-generation iPhone Air. Why the drastic change in strategy? It may be due to the ongoing memory shortage, which has made just about everything more expensive. In June, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that Apple would raise product prices to keep up with manufacturing costs. “Our assumption is that they're going to be launching three models in the fall, the premium side of the models of the 18 series,” says Nabila Popal, a senior director of data and analytics at IDC. “Then the mid/budget devices will be launched in the spring.” Popal says it's a smart strategic move because Apple is aiming to spread out its revenue between a usually very strong fourth quarter and a typically much weaker spring quarter the following year. Apple’s portfolio has also expanded, and the iPhone Pro and Pro Max lineup are more enticing for people already prepared to spend the money on a new iPhone. When components become more expensive, companies have three real options: Eat the costs, raise prices, or, as Apple seems to be doing, lean into it. By moving its cheaper options to a later date, Apple can drum up excitement for its bigger, better, pricier offerings. When it charges more for those, it is likely to be less off-putting than making a cheap phone even more expensive. It’s part of a “premiumization” of devices, as Popal calls it, that Apple hopes to leverage and build hype for its pricier options. Shawn DuBravac, chief economist at the Global Electronics Association, tells WIRED he is optimistic about what these kinds of rising prices ultimately mean for customers. “Throughout the history of time, the deflationary pressures of technology have always flowed to the consumer,” DuBravac says. “I'm confident that will be the case again. It just will take some time for the markets to solidify.” In other words, new technologies launch with a high price, but manufacturing efficiencies and competition inevitably drive costs down for consumers. That may not be the case anytime soon for folding phones, which are seeing higher prices than ever. Samsung’s entire 2026 Galaxy Z folding smartphone range saw price increases, as did Google’s new Pixel 11 Pro Fold, and Motorola’s Razr 2026 models. Apple’s folding iPhone is rumored to cost around $2,000. To help mitigate those high costs, Apple is turning to financing options and trade-in programs. In July, the company launched an iPhone leasing program that lets people pay a monthly fee to rent the newest iPhones, then swap them out when a new device releases. The program will undoubtedly help more people afford the newest devices, but ownership advocates have criticized it, saying it keeps you from truly owning and managing your device. It also fits Apple’s broader effort to turn all of its products into a subscription service. “The way most consumers buy Apple phones is through financing or trade-in programs,” Popal says. “We can expect a lot more aggressive trade-ins to help cushion that.” Thanks to the memory crisis and price increases, all smartphones are getting more costly to make. Less expensive phones become less appealing for manufacturers to prioritize, and leading smartphone brands have started to see them as far less economical to produce. On the flip side, demand for refurbished devices has been climbing for a while now, with sales of used devices growing even as new phone sales slow down. More people are looking to save money or purchase more eco-friendly products. “The days of the cheap smartphone are over,” Popal says.

entry.title: Microsoft’s latest moves suggest Xbox Cloud Gaming is slipping out of the spotlight — and the strategy shift feels impossible to ignore - Windows Central
entry.body: Microsoft’s recent decisions paint a clear picture — Xbox Cloud Gaming is no longer the future the company once promised Xbox's cloud gaming hourly limit rates have been met with derision in the fanbase, and have highlighted gaps between other services. Xbox Cloud Gaming has essentially been put out to pasture, with Microsoft intent on including hourly limits on the service. From November 2026, Microsoft will impose a 15-hour cap on Xbox Game Pass Ultimate users playing cloud games, as well as a 10-hour cap on Premium, and 5 hours on Essential. It's a huge climbdown from the previous "unlimited" access Xbox Cloud Gaming granted, and an indictment of the business model in general. Microsoft has rolled out Xbox Cloud Gaming to LG, Samsung, and now TCL TVs as of today, which makes for some awkward timing. The limits have been met with derision both within and without the Xbox fanbase, and have shone a spotlight on where Xbox is falling short here. NVIDIA GeForce Now will extend its value over Xbox Cloud Gaming Already the market leader, NVIDIA GeForce Now introduced hourly limits a few months ago in response to some criticism, although the limits GFN offers are far more generous than what Microsoft has proposed here. On GFN's highest tiers, you get 100 hours, with some hours rolling over to the next month too. Not only that, but NVIDIA GeForce Now also just offers a generally higher-quality experience, with better bitrates, latency, and stability. Xbox Game Pass had it beat before on usability, though, with a more console-like interface and more TV-friendly apps. Game Pass also comes with a larger upfront library of games, whereas NVIDIA GeForce Now, for the most part, is made up of games you've already purchased from Steam. The issue for me is ... 15 hours just isn't enough to complete the vast majority of decent games these days. Fable is supposedly around 30 hours long for a completionist playthrough. Will Xbox Cloud Gaming users be expected to spread their session across two months to finish the game? Microsoft is going to offer per-hour passes to boost how much access you have, but we've not really seen the pricing yet. I have a feeling they won't be cheap. Xbox Remote Play could be a solution ... but it seems to be abandoned We live in a weird dichotomy right now, driven by the AI component crisis. Microsoft is buying up all the memory for its AI push and leaving Xbox with scraps on the side. That extends to Xbox Cloud Gaming servers too, and while they can be used for AI workloads off-peak, I'm told, they're obviously not specialized for that type of work. Either way, servers break down and wear out; they need to be replaced regularly. Running servers 24/7 is an expensive business on the component side, even before you start thinking about electricity and water for cooling. A chap on X (Twitter) sent me a link to an Xbox Player Voice feedback item that laments the quality of Xbox Remote Play. You can effectively turn a home Xbox Series X|S console into a "personal cloud server" and have it stream your games over a viable Wi-Fi network. The problem is, despite being similar hardware, Xbox Remote Play is inexplicably locked to 1080p. Xbox Cloud Gaming on Xbox Game Pass Ultimate offers 1440p with higher bitrates, too. There's no real reason why, at least in the case of the Xbox Series X, we shouldn't be able to get a better Xbox Remote Play experience. But that doesn't exactly solve things for users who rely entirely on Xbox Cloud Gaming ... Cloud-first gamers who bought an Xbox Ally base model or other cloud-first devices like the Logitech G Cloud are pretty much screwed by this change — unless Microsoft does something to improve Xbox Remote Play. That is, of course, presuming they even own an Xbox Series X|S, both of which are now insanely expensive. None of this really makes a lot of sense, does it? Update: Since writing this piece, it seems Microsoft began testing 1440p on Xbox Remote Play too on the Xbox Insider program's Alpha Ring, which is a huge win. But there's still not a lot of information about whether they're going to respond to the backlash about cloud usage limits. I'll try and get more info later about exactly what we can expect from Xbox Remote Play. Xbox Cloud Gaming is another victim of the RAMpocalypse I was recently told by Microsoft figures that, given compute demands for AI, Xbox Cloud Gaming is effectively losing money when used beyond 15 hours per month. When you have Azure server rack space being used for anything other than AI, it seems Microsoft isn't particularly sentimental towards the idea anymore. Microsoft has been on an economic grind for Xbox over the past few months, "restructuring" the org to ensure that it sends a bigger accountability margin back to the mothership. That's meant mass Xbox layoffs and cancellations of projects, and a more aggressive posture towards easy wins. Xbox Cloud Gaming clearly isn't an easy win in this new reality. If 15 hours is the cap that prevents the service from being unprofitable ... perhaps the business model was never really viable in the first place. Xbox Cloud Gaming isn't exactly struggling in a vacuum, though. Other companies that rely entirely on cloud inference seem to be struggling. Whether it's Roblox or Twitch, the era of "cheap cloud" seems to be over — alongside video game consoles themselves, and consumer hardware in general, seemingly. Either way, I don't see how you can plausibly expect people to use cloud gaming as a primary vehicle with such a strict limit. Microsoft isn't able to get Xbox hardware stock to most of the world either. you start wondering why Microsoft is so eager to let a literal billion Windows 11 users burn cash on a pyre for free access to Microsoft Copilot ... but wants to charge out the nose for Xbox Cloud Gaming? It's a pretty clear admission that they don't see much of a future for cloud gaming in general. Or perhaps it's just more AI psychosis. Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more. Jez Corden is the Executive Editor at Windows Central, focusing primarily on all things Xbox and gaming. Jez is known for breaking exclusive news and analysis as relates to the Microsoft ecosystem — while being powered by tea. Follow on X.com/JezCorden and tune in to the XB2 Podcast, all about, you guessed it, Xbox! entry.title: From chess to battle for pole, Gasly has Russell covered at Monza
entry.body: From chess to battle for pole, Gasly has Russell covered at Monza - Published A quarter of an hour before the qualifying session which delivered the biggest surprise pole position in Formula 1 for years, Alpine's Pierre Gasly was playing online chess with Mercedes driver George Russell and winning. "I must say before the quali, I felt pretty confident," the Frenchman said, "because I was picking piece by piece after piece." Gasly's performance coach Ben Thorne was watching. "For a fun story," Gasly said, "Ben told me, 'OK, well, you're getting George here, but he's going to get you in a few minutes.'" Gasly said he reacted with a swear word but he was smiling as he recalled the moment. "Turned out that it worked out well. So yeah, it's been fun," he added. Russell, who lines up second to Gasly, was laughing about it. "He beat me there," the Briton said, "and I thought, 'Well, I think I'll beat you in qualifying,' and here we are, he's ahead of me again." No-one - especially not Gasly nor his Alpine team - would have predicted the 30-year-old would end up on pole in Monza on Saturday, even though his only win in F1 came at this exact track six years ago. That victory, in the middle of F1's bizarre, spectator-less pandemic season, owed a lot to luck - a remarkable race that ended up with Gasly, then driving for Red Bull's Toro Rosso team, taking a restart from third place and Lance Stroll going off ahead of him on the first lap to gift him the lead once Lewis Hamilton had served a penalty. This pole was not like that. It was absolutely earned on merit. The Alpine has strong straight-line speed with a low-downforce-leaning aerodynamic design. The car - which has a Mercedes engine, the best in the field - has looked quick all weekend. It had an upgrade that lifted its performance at the last race in the Netherlands. And Gasly and his team absolutely nailed qualifying, while all the usual leading contenders had scrappy sessions one way or another. "Monza is a bit of unique track as we know," Gasly said. "It definitely exceeded all our expectations. "Since this morning, the pace has been better. We managed to make a good step from P3 to quali and I think slightly bigger than the other guys around us. "Straight from Q1, we were a bit surprised to see us up there. But then I was P1 in Q1, then P4 in Q2. I didn't want to get too excited but then first run in Q3, I was third again. "And then I felt, 'OK, well, I really have a shot at it.' It's probably the first time I really get a true chance and tried to leave everything I had out there. "It was quite hectic through Ascari and Parabolica. I don't think there was definitely much (left) in there. And crossing the line, I knew it will be one of these laps that will be rewarded. But to the point to get to the pole position, I didn't expect that." - Alpine's Gasly beats Russell to stunning Monza pole - Published5 hours ago 'From being down to being on top of the world' Gasly is well liked within the paddock, and has many friends among the drivers, but he has long been one of F1's forgotten heroes, regardless of that win six years ago. A Red Bull protege, his time in the works team in 2019 did not work out. Like so many since, he was crushed by Max Verstappen, and demoted back to the second team after half a season. After sticking with Red Bull for three more years, he was given an opportunity with Alpine, and he hoped a move to a factory team would be his making. But Alpine have stumbled since, until finally showing signs of a revival this season, following Renault's decision to abandon its F1 engine project and switch to Mercedes customer engines. The team had been making headlines already this weekend. On Friday, Gasly lost the podium at Monaco to which he had been promoted after Alpine won an appeal against two penalties for pit-lane speeding, when the FIA court of appeal reinstated the punishment. A few hours later, de facto team boss Flavio Briatore caused an eruption in a news conference when he alleged one of the four judges in the case had "links" with McLaren. It was a claim that appeared to lack any substance, based as it was on a charity event in California in 2018 at which the judge in question had been present and to which a local McLaren garage had apparently donated "two or three" cars. And Briatore provided no evidence to back up the insinuation he was making. The claim was described as "insulting" in that news conference by McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, and afterwards it became clear that McLaren were furious about what Briatore had said on apparently the most flimsy of bases. Then, on Saturday, a rare statement from the FIA court of appeal refuted the allegation and any "questions (about) the independence and impartiality of the judges". The court of appeal verdict made a lot of sense. It left many questions about the controversy of the pit-lane penalties in Monaco, but at least it ensured all drivers who had been given them had been treated equitably - notwithstanding the fact that it seems none of them should have received the penalties. Regardless of the questionable nature of Briatore's comments, Alpine were unhappy about losing their Monaco podium, feeling that they had been given two penalties unjustly when their evidence showed Gasly had never been over the pit-lane speeding limit. Managing director Steve Nielsen told Sky Sports: "Two or three days ago, we were on the floor. It is really from being down to being on top of the world in just two days and it is amazing. We need to soak it up and make the best of it. "Pierre is a class act. If you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year. "We haven't always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have, he has delivered, particularly earlier in the season, So to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful." In qualifying, Gasly was positioned second last in the train of cars on the final qualifying run, the absolute optimum place in terms of a slipstream. 'Bit of a mess' compromises Russell Others, meanwhile, were compromised in one way or another, including the favourite for pole, Russell, when Verstappen disrupted Mercedes' attempts to have team-mate Kimi Antonelli tow the Briton by getting between the two silver cars at the end of their out laps. "We had a bit of a mess with Verstappen entering the lap," Russell said. "He wanted to go for the tow, Kimi was there as well, and I did my lap a second and a half behind Max, which wasn't ideal. "It takes nothing away from what Pierre achieved because, as he said, they were flying all day, quickest in Q1 and right up there from the beginning. So I'm happy for Pierre and, of course, disappointed we weren't on pole ourselves. However, great place to start for tomorrow." Russell acknowledged after qualifying what is at stake for him on Sunday. He goes into the race 59 championship points behind leader Antonelli, who has pretty much had his measure all season. But he has a golden opportunity to make up ground on the Italian, who is due to start 20th because of a grid penalty for exceeding his engine allowance. Russell said: "The win is going to be very important tomorrow but I'm more pleased about the performance. Since the summer break, every lap I have been in the top three positions, while I had that tough run of form before the break when every lap wasn't in the top five." Antonelli is expected easily to get back into the top six or so, but that would still allow Russell to make a substantial dent in his advantage. Given Russell has his own grid penalty looming within a couple of races for the same reason, it is imperative for his title hopes that he does so. Italian Grand Prix Race start at 14:00 BST on Sunday Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra 2; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app On Friday, Gasly did not appear to have the race speed to challenge the top teams, so even though overtaking is harder at Monza than might be expected given its long straights, he knows it will be tough to win the race. "Obviously not to the pace of these guys around us, but we seem to have picked up more pace from yesterday to today," Gasly said. "So we'll obviously give our best shot and see what we can get out of it." Aside from Gasly, Russell's main opposition is likely to come from Ferrari, who for the third race in a row seemed to fumble a better qualifying result for operational reasons. It was a bad time to do it again, as they debuted their upgraded engine at their home race. After both cars came perilously close to being knocked out in the second part of qualifying, Charles Leclerc left the pits in the final session while Lewis Hamilton had no wheels on his car, so the seven-time champion was far from best placed for his run in terms of the slipstream. Leclerc and Hamilton will start third and fourth after McLaren's Oscar Piastri was given a three-place grid penalty for impeding Red Bull's Liam Lawson. Hamilton - like Russell, 59 points behind Antonelli - seemed to imply after qualifying that he felt the team should prioritise his hopes over Leclerc's, even if he could not quite bring himself to say it outright. "(Piastri's penalty) puts us in (with a) fighting chance, hopefully, with George," Hamilton said. "That's one Mercedes up front, so hopefully that gives us a chance to work as a team to try and topple them. "We're at a point in the year where 59 points is a huge - huge - deficit to recover from, especially when Mercedes continue to be the leaders in speed. "So yeah, we do have to work as a team. if and when that would ever change... we'll find out, but all I can do is just try to arrive and do the best job I can." entry.title: Christian Gonzalez doesn’t commit to playing season opener - NBC Sports
entry.body: Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez still doesn’t have a contract extension, and with the season opener only four days away, he isn’t not committing to playing without one. Gonzalez continues to take a day-to-day approach. “I’m focused on today,” Gonzalez said, via Doug Kyed of the Boston Herald. “Right now, it is practice in what, a couple, 30 minutes, 40 minutes. Worried on that right now, so we’ll focus on that.” Gonzalez answered “I don’t know” when asked if contract talks were progressing. The Seahawks recently signed cornerback Devon Witherspoon to a four-year, $132 million deal, which should provide a template for the Patriots. Gonzalez and Witherspoon have the same agent, Reggie Johnson. Gonzalez is under contract for the next two seasons and is scheduled to make a base salary of $2.259 million this season. The 17th overall pick in 2023, he made second-team All-Pro in 2024 and the Pro Bowl in 2025. He has totaled 145 tackles, two interceptions, 24 pass breakups and a sack in three seasons. He said Thursday he is “still frustrated” a deal isn’t done.

The newcomers are highlighted by TCU transfer quarterback Josh Hoover, Michigan State transfer wide receiver Nick Marsh, and Boston College transfer running back Turbo Richard; all of which were a focal point in the Indiana offense. Hoover finished 13/16, for 231 passing yards and four touchdowns. Leading the way in the receivers' room was Charlie Becker (64 yards, 2 touchdowns), Nick Marsh (17 yards, 1 touchdown), Davion Chandler (42 yards, 1 touchdown), and Tyler Morris (35 yards). Isaiah Jones led the Indiana defense with 12 tackles, while Byron Baldwin and Rolijah Hardy each added seven. Kansas State transfer Tobi Osunsanmi finished with two TFLs, and Cincinnati transfer Quan Sanks had a late-game interception. North Texas was led by former Indiana and Center Grove quarterback Tayven Jackson. After being named the starter at the end of August, Jackson had a strong start to his fifth collegiate season as he finished with 22/28 for 192 yards and one interception. entry.title: Wigan crush Leeds to move closer to winning shield
entry.body: Wigan crush Leeds to move closer to winning shield - Published Betfred Super League Leeds (8) 8 Tries: Handley Goals: Connor 2 Wigan (16) 40 Tries: Keighran 3, Daniel, Marshall, French, Field Goals: Keighran 6 Wigan Warriors produced an outstanding display on the big occasion once again as they defeated Leeds Rhinos to take a giant step towards lifting the League Leaders' Shield. The Warriors leapfrogged the Rhinos to move two points clear at the top and if they match Leeds' result in the final game of the regular season on Friday, they will claim their second piece of silverware of the year. It was their 14th straight Super League win and it is hard to imagine them not beating Catalans Dragons at home to finish the job, with the Rhinos welcoming Hull FC at the same time. Two early tries from Adam Keighran put them in charge at a sold-out Headingley before Ash Handley got Leeds on the scoreboard before the break. Teenage winger Austin Daniel scored only his second Super League try to restore a 10-point advantage before fellow winger Liam Marshall crossed early in the second half to put Wigan firmly in control. Their defence remained resolute as Leeds tried to get back into the game, and further tries from star backs Bevan French and Jai Field and a hat-trick from Keighran showed why they will be strong favourites to win the Grand Final at Old Trafford on 3 October. - Wakefield stay in top-four hunt with win over Wire - Published5 hours ago - York run in five tries for dream win over Catalans - Published2 hours ago - Women's Super League: Wigan thrash Leeds to storm on - Published3 hours ago The Rhinos have been top since May in pursuit of their first silverware since 2020 â a long wait for one of rugby league's powerhouses - while they have not finished top of Super League since 2015. But the Warriors have been in their rearview mirror as they have been imperious through the summer, on the back of a winning streak which started more than three months ago with a dismantling of Hull KR in the Challenge Cup final at Wembley. After a shaky spring, Wigan have been back to their best as they chase a treble, to go with the quadruple they secured two years ago. Super League's leading try scorer, Maika Sivo, did not make the Leeds squad after recovering from a broken arm, but there was a setback for the hosts early in the game as full-back Lachie Miller limped off with a hamstring injury. With the Rhinos reshuffling, Wigan pounced as the great teams do. Sharp handling from French and Keighran got the ball to teenage winger Austin Daniel who, on just his fourth league appearance, showed a turn of pace down the wing and then awareness to set up Keighran to score. Oliver Partington had a try disallowed, but the Warriors were not to be denied as French's bullet pass put fellow Australian Keighran over again. Leeds were stunned but found a response as Connor hoisted a high kick which was brilliantly caught and then touched down by captain Handley. They were right back in the contest, but French simply dipped into his box of tricks to move Wigan further clear as the stand-off threw a sensational pass that took out three defenders and gave Daniel a walk-in. Connor kicked a goal on the stroke of half-time to reduce the gap to eight points. But the visitors claimed the first score of the second half through Marshall's trademark finish in the left corner, although the unhappy hosts believed Wigan had knocked on in the build-up. There was a hint of desperation as Leeds tried to force their way back into the game, but there were no chinks in the Warriors defence and their class was on show at the other end. Harry Smith's clever kick found space and French, on his 200th career appearance, was first on to it, before Field's dazzling feet grabbed Wigan's sixth try. Keighran then completed his hat-trick as the clock was ticking down to cap another glorious night for this storied club. 'We let the club down' - reaction Leeds Rhinos head coach Brad Arthur told BBC Radio Leeds: "We're disappointed, we didn't put our best foot forward tonight. It was a big occasion for the club and not through effort, but we let ourselves down and we let the club down. "It's certainly not over, but we've got to dust ourselves down. We've got a big game next week and we need to regain some form. On Lachlan Miller's injury: "It's not great. He's obviously got to go and have scans, but I think he's torn his hamstring. We'll have to wait and see. "It's hard to replace a player of his quality, but then it's hard to replace a full-back, they're so integral to your defensive line, the organisation of that and how he returns the ball. "We were a bit disjointed from it, but we've got to be a bit more resilient." Leeds: Miller; Hall, Bird, Handley, Newman; Croft, Connor; Oledzki, O'Connor, Jenkins, Watkins, Hankinson, Cassell. Interchanges: C Smith, Lodge, Lloyd, Holroyd. Wigan: Field; Daniel, Keighran, Eckersley, Marhsall; French, H Smith; Havard, O'Neill, Thompson, McDermott, Partington, Ellis. Interchanges: Nsemba, Walters, Mago, Kerr.
entry.summary: Wigan Warriors move within touching distance of winning the League Leaders' Shield after a superb victory at closest rivals Leeds Rhinos.

entry.title: Robert Pattinson Kisses Suki Waterhouse as ‘Primetime’ Rocks Venice With 7-Minute Standing Ovation - Variety
entry.body: “Primetime,” a thriller starring Robert Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, made its debut at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday to an enthusiastic seven-minute ovation. Venice went fully in for Pattinson’s immersive performance as Hansen, the “Dateline” journalist and host who sets out to make television history with “To Catch a Predator.” And one of the biggest fans in attendance? Pattinson’s partner Suki Waterhouse, who cheered perhaps loudest during the seven-minute standing ovation and leaned forward and kissed Pattinson on the lips as the crowd applauded his tour-de-force performance. (In Venice, actors are seated in the front row of the balcony and their partners must sit a row behind them.) As the ovation stretched into its sixth minute, the audience began chanting for director Lance Oppenheim and singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers, who makes her acting debut in the film. Skyler Gisondo and Merritt Wever also star. Based on Luke Dittrich’s 2007 Esquire article “Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die,” “Primetime” follows the production of the popular series, in which Hansen attempted to confront child sexual predators in complex sting operations. Popular on Variety Massive crowds outside the Palazzo del Cinema were chanting “Robert! Robert!” as they baked in the sun on a brutally hot Saturday afternoon. Pattinson, Gisando and Bridgers dutifully signed autographs and posed for tons of selfies with fans while Waterhouse made small talk with producers off to the side of the action. Pattinson dabbed the sweat off his forehead with napkins before posing for a cast photo. Former NBC chief Jeff Zucker, who appears in the movie as himself, also walked the red carpet, as did producer Ari Aster. “Primetime” marks Oppenheim’s feature debut, having previously helmed acclaimed documentaries such as “Some Kind of Heaven” and HBO’s “Ren Faire.” A24 will release “Primetime” in theaters on Sept. Hansen has been vocal in his criticisms about “Primetime,” saying he wasn’t involved in the creative process and hadn’t seen the movie. He called Pattinson’s portrayal “overly dramatic” and questioned the studio’s “motive” in dramatizing the making of the hit reality series. Hansen has also stressed that “Primetime” isn’t a literal account of his career and that he wasn’t consulted during the making of the movie. “He’s saying things I never said and doing things I never did, and that’s not who I am. I’m a nice guy, except when it comes to criminals and predators,” Hansen previously said. “I think people should remember that it is a work of fiction, only based on real-life events.” At a press conference earlier on Saturday, Pattinson suggested that Hansen could come around once he sees the film. “Obviously, I hope he likes the movie,” Pattinson said. “There’s something electrifying about him. I would hope the amount of inspiration his character has given a lot of people for years is some kind of compliment.” “Primetime” continues a banner year for Pattinson, who stars in such high-profile films as this spring’s indie hit “The Drama,” Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster “The Odyssey” and Denis Villeneuve’s upcoming tentpole “Dune: Part III.” And Pattinson’s schedule remains packed: He jetted to Lido from London, where he is currently filming “The Batman: Part II,” reprising his role as reclusive billionaire-turned-vigilante Bruce Wayne. “When you get the momentum going, it’s strangely not that hard,” Pattinson said at the presser. Plus, he joked, “I just had a baby. I had no desire to go out at night. So suddenly I had twice as much time, which was helpful.”

entry.title: ‘Evil Dead’ Star Bruce Campbell Says He Has 5 Years to Live After Incurable Cancer Diagnosis: I’m ‘Dying’ but ‘I’m Moving On’
entry.body: “Evil Dead” star Bruce Campbell is opening up about his battle with cancer, revealing that he’s been given about five years to live. Back in March, Campbell revealed he had been diagnosed with a cancer that was “treatable but not curable.” “These days, when someone is having a health issue, it’s referred to as an ‘opportunity,’ so let’s go with that — I’m having one of those,” he wrote on X in March. “It’s also called a type of cancer that’s ‘treatable’ not ‘curable.’ I apologize if that’s a shock – it was to me too.” Campbell didn’t go into detail about what type of cancer he’d been diagnosed with, but wrote that “professionally, a few things will have to change. Appearances and cons and work in general need to take back seat to treatment. My plan is to get as well as I possibly can over the summer so that I can tour with my new movie ‘Ernie & Emma’ this fall.” Popular on Variety On Wednesday’s episode of “The Adam Carolla Show,” Campbell opened up more about his diagnosis and treatment while also discussing his new movie. “I’m in a five-year prognosis,” he said. “With the type of cancer that I have, which I don’t want to get into, the current thing is a five-year deal.” When Carolla asked if that meant Campbell had five years to live, the actor replied “give or take.” “It’s a fascinating thing that takes place because [cancer] messes with your head, too. I’ve decided though, pretty specifically, to live with it, not die from it,” he added. “You can go down a massive rabbit hole. The cancer rabbit hole is enormous. You can go into focus groups of 10,000 guys who have exactly what you have. I won’t touch it with a 10-foot pole.” Campbell serves as director, writer, producer and lead actor in “Ernie & Emma,” in which he plays a widower scattering his late wife’s ashes, reflecting on their relationship together and confronting his grief. “It’s a very fascinating time of having a movie about a guy who’s spreading his wife’s ashes, who died, made by a guy who’s dying,” he told Carolla. entry.title: Andrew Scott Has Waited His Whole Career for a Role Like ‘Elsinore.’ Can Focus and the Bard Anoint Him With an Oscar?
entry.body: Andrew Scott is the prince of Telluride. There are performances that feel like a reckoning, and performances that feel like a resurrection. Andrew Scott’s work in “Elsinore,” which had its world premiere Friday night at the Telluride Film Festival, is somehow both — a great actor playing a great actor as the curtain starts to fall, and refusing to let it. Directed by Simon Stone and written by Stephen Beresford, “Elsinore” tells the true story of Ian Charleson, the Scottish “Chariots of Fire” star who spent the last year of his life playing Hamlet at London’s National Theatre as AIDS was quietly taking his life. He died in 1990 at 40. His Hamlet — hailed then as one of the finest of its generation — became a farewell disguised as a role. The casting is too perfect to be accidental. Scott is himself a celebrated London Hamlet, here playing a man whose Hamlet was his last act of defiance. “Elsinore” is, at its heart, a love letter to actors — to the craft as vocation, to the courage of standing in the light when the body is failing. And a milestone waits inside the role. No openly gay man has ever won the Oscar for best actor, and Scott could very well become the first. Popular on Variety Make no mistake, this is the role of Scott’s career and it lands him toward the forefront of a best actor conversation he has been circling for years. He has never been Oscar-nominated — a fact that curdled into open disdain when the Academy passed over his shattering turn in “All of Us Strangers.” “Elsinore” is the correction: he captures Charleson’s wit, vanity, terror and grace inside the same breath and in the final stretch, he nails Hamlet’s readiness measured against a dying man’s own — the sustained high-wire work voters still see behind their eyes in January. It’s also a role the Academy has never resisted. Voters are reliably moved by the actor staring down the barrel of death — Tom Hanks in “Philadelphia” (1993), Matthew McConaughey in “Dallas Buyers Club” (2013) and Anthony Hopkins vanishing into dementia in “The Father” (2020). “Elsinore” hands Scott the AIDS-era variation, with the added charge of real history — a story to discover even for those who think they already know it. Charleson was a real man and a real actor, dying as he did, playing Hamlet as he did. That is not a fact that asks for votes so much as one that issues a commandment, and I dare any Academy member not to see the worth in honoring such a life through a vessel as gifted as Scott. Then there is Olivia Colman, who has entered her “Maggie Smith” era and is plainly having the time of her life. Her supporting turn as Charleson’s doctor is all steel and mischief — grumpy one moment, gutting the next — the work of a past winner (“The Favourite”) who keeps finding registers no one knew she had. It belongs in the supporting actress conversation without an asterisk, the season’s most quotable grande dame showcase since Smith herself. Watch, too, for Billie Piper, as a casting director and Charleson’s confidant, who does the quietest and maybe the most surprising work in the film. Stone directed her to an Olivier Award in his radical stage “Yerma,” and their reunion could carry her into a film-awards conversation for the first time. If Focus campaigns her with nerve, she’s a supporting actress spoiler nobody is clocking just yet. The rest of the craft work is impeccable. Stefan Gregory’s score rips — propulsive where you brace for a sonorous monologue, tender where you expect something loud. Stone directs with a theater maker’s reverence for the actor’s face; Beresford, who wrote “Pride,” has built a script funnier than any logline would suggest and gutting exactly when it must be. One curious wrinkle: the script credit reads “based on an idea by Ethan Silverman,” which raises the kind of question pundits love — a “Barbie”-style scramble over whether the Academy files it as original or adapted. The WGA has designated it original. What ultimately matters is this: is it Scott only, or should we brace for more? A lead performance, fully embraced, can drag a whole film up the ballot. Sandra Bullock’s “The Blind Side” was beloved enough to pull the movie into best picture — its only other nomination — and she won. “Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close” managed the same trick, riding supporting actor nominee Max von Sydow to a best picture berth; it won neither, but von Sydow was plainly the runner-up to Christopher Plummer’s winning turn in “Beginners” — itself that film’s only nomination. Then there are the critically adored turns that stand alone. Colin Firth in Tom Ford’s “A Single Man” managed exactly one nomination — his — and lost. A year later, folded inside the 12-nomination embrace of “The King’s Speech,” he walked away with the prize. A lone acting nod is a precarious perch, and Scott will need more than that to convert his into a trophy. “Elsinore” likely needs Colman and Piper in supporting, Beresford’s screenplay on the ballot — or perhaps techs like makeup and editing — and even a best picture berth. A great performance gets you nominated; a film full of them gets you onstage. This can be Focus Features’ specialty. No specialty distributor has been better over the last 25 years at minting best actor winners from biopics — Adrien Brody (“The Pianist”), Sean Penn (“Milk”), Matthew McConaughey (“Dallas Buyers Club”), Eddie Redmayne (“The Theory of Everything”) and Gary Oldman (“Darkest Hour”) — five men, each playing a real one, each launched off a fall-festival bow and a patient platform release. And every one of those films was a best picture nominee. “Elsinore” follows the blueprint to the letter. The material carries its own Oscar pedigree — and Focus is riding it. Last winter the studio won its first best actress Oscar with Jessie Buckley in “Hamnet,” the story of the family loss that gave the world “Hamlet”; a few years earlier, Kenneth Branagh, cinema’s foremost Shakespearean, took original screenplay for the Focus release “Belfast.” The Academy’s affection reaches back further, to the wins “Shakespeare in Love” minted for Gwyneth Paltrow and Judi Dench. Now, two years running, the studio has a “Hamlet” in the race. The Bard has been good to this address. Hamlet’s final words are “the rest is silence.” “Elsinore,” and the actor at its center, make a beautiful liar of the line. On Friday night in the mountains, the rest was a room on its feet and an actor, at last, getting the reception for the role he was born to play. Read Variety’s review of “Elsinore” here.

entry.title: Hey, Oscars: No Sympathy Required to Give Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ the Consideration It Deserves
entry.body: Let’s dispense with the suspense. Mike Leigh has been nominated for an Academy Award seven times and has won it zero times. He has a Palme d’Or, a Golden Lion, five decades of films that taught generations of actors what unglamorous truth looks like and one of the most distinctive bodies of work in modern British cinema. What he does not have is an Oscar — and based on the reviews and reactions out of the Telluride Film Festival, where the film bowed Friday night, it’s about damn time he got one. “Tender Loving Care” arrives carrying the weight none of Leigh’s previous films did. At 83, and contending with myosotis, a muscle-wasting condition that kept him from his own Telluride premiere, Leigh has said this is most likely his last film. Bleecker Street opens it Dec. 4 after a fall festival run the industry reserves for titles it takes seriously. Popular on Variety That makes the season’s obvious question unavoidable: What should the Academy do with Mike Leigh’s final film? The answer is not — give him an Oscar because he is 83. It is — watch the movie, and you’ll see why you’d want to. “Tender Loving Care” does not need a sympathy campaign. It is vintage Leigh — wry, melancholy, humane, alert to the small emotional humiliations that become, over the course of a life, the events that define us. Kate O’Flynn’s Amy anchors it — an Emmy nominee for “Widow’s Bay,” and when the trophies are handed out Sept. 14, very possibly a winner — a social worker steadying a father in decline, gutted by a breakup and kept upright by wine and by Rosie, the live-wire best friend played exquisitely by Alice Bailey Johnson. Marion Bailey, as Amy’s mother, has already emerged from Telluride as a standout, a veteran thespian never given her proper due. A film about the daily labor of caring for people, made by a filmmaker who has spent 50 years caring, without vanity, about the interior lives most movies never bother to notice. It’s a perfect bookend to a career — and it closes on perhaps the most haunting final shot of any film in a decade. There’s a smaller bookend folded inside it, too: Leigh gave O’Flynn her first job, on “Happy-Go-Lucky,” at 21. She returns for his last. That sets up a campaign with an unusual shape and real vigor. Leigh carries the legacy narrative, but the film has to prove first that the work is competitive in a year crowded with filmmakers nursing overdue stories of their own. So the cleanest argument for Leigh is historical, not sentimental. Seven nominations and zero wins is a remarkable record. Twice — for “Secrets & Lies” and “Vera Drake” — the Academy nominated Leigh for both writing and directing in the same year, the dual embrace it reserves for its favorites. It has honored him again and again without ever closing the final distance. This is not an artist who spent a career waiting for his first invitation. The performances could help carry him there. O’Flynn and Bailey have the most obvious pathways, though where their teams ultimately campaign is still being sorted — and pundits will argue over where the two should land, which is rarely where they actually do. When two women read as co-leads, the Academy has grown allergic to rewarding both in the same category: the last time it nominated two lead actresses from a single film was “Thelma & Louise,” Susan Sarandon and Geena Davis, in 1991. So I’d bet the campaign splits them — O’Flynn, the anchor, in lead actress and Bailey in supporting. It should be duly noted, Bailey Johnson would be a worthy option to join whichever lady decides on the supporting campaign and as the ailing father, Paul Jesson is also incredibly rich and dynamic and would be worthy of consideration. But Bleecker Street will have to decide where to spend. An intimate British drama cannot campaign on every front with the force of a studio tent-pole. That is where the festival strategy matters. Toronto should widen the critical and industry conversation. The New York Film Festival drops the film into the center of the American awards ecosystem. The distributor’s job now is turning that accumulation into industry votes. There is a trap in the “last film” framing, too. Leigh’s age and health explain the stakes of the moment, but they should never become the reason to vote. The Academy has a long, familiar habit of honoring artists after the fact. The more respectful campaign makes the case while the artist is still here — still working at full command of his gifts. This is not a plea for a career-achievement handout. It is simply an argument that the film should earn the consideration on its own merits, and that a body claiming to honor the year’s best would embarrass itself to overlook a master telling us, gently, that he is done. He named the film “Tender Loving Care.” The least the Academy can do is extend some.

entry.title: Dolly Parton's sister slams 'fake AI garbage' in the wake of icon's death - USA Today
entry.body: Dolly Parton's sister slams 'fake AI garbage' in the wake of icon's death Dolly Parton's sister Stella Parton is condemning the deluge of misinformation being spread in the wake of the country star's death. The younger Parton, 77, took time from her morning “coffee hour" Friday, Sept. 4, to express how such online negativity has taken an emotional toll on her family as they continue grieving the “I Will Always Love You” singer, who died Aug. In a two-slide statement on Instagram, Stella Parton first thanked the "genuine" supporters who have been kind and respectful during the Parton family's bereavement, then addressed the bad-faith social media users who have been anything but considerate. Stella Parton slams 'fake AI garbage' following Dolly Parton's death “Sadly, because of the way our lives have been lived in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers,” she wrote. “There is a tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted everyday and it’s been challenging to absorb and or ignore.” “As time passes, those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others on a daily basis will move on to the next stampede of endless misinformation,” Stella Parton added, imploring fans to "show more compassion and wisdom as we move forward in life." Rather than indulge in "clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets" concerning the "Jolene" singer's death, Stella Parton urged fans to "use my sister's life as an example for tolerance and respect toward others." As a final point of advice, she reminded fans to remember this: "At the end of the day or the end of a life, how will you feel about yourself? It's not about what other individuals you will never meet think of you!" Stella Parton's message comes mere days after the "Steel Magnolias" actress' star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame was allegedly vandalized. (Her star has since been replaced and will reopen to the public Sept. 14.) Stella Parton remembers Dolly Parton, recalls icon's final days The "I Want to Hold You in My Dreams Tonight" singer has been outspoken about grieving her sister's loss. When the news broke, she released a heartfelt tribute to her big sister, recalling their Tuesday morning routine and the Queen of Country's final days. "What the world saw is exactly who she was, so much so, she told me recently that if there was no hope for her, she would still allow her medical team to try experimental drugs in the hope of helping others in the future," she wrote on Facebook. "My sister was always thinking of others and if you want to honor her legacy, show more kindness, lift others up and give more of your time and resources as she continued to do to the very end," she added. "Dolly loved the world and everyone in it." How did Dolly Parton die? Parton died aged 80 on Aug. 25, following a private cancer battle, her representatives confirmed to USA TODAY. The "9 to 5" star's death came 16 months after the loss of Dean, who died in March 2025 at age 82. Her nephew Bryan Seaver, who is the son of the singer's sister Cassie, delivered the news of her death via video announcement on social media, per her wishes. Her niece Lainey Mae Parton confirmed on social media that Parton had been laid to rest on Aug. 28 in a small and private memorial held for her immediate family.

entry.body: Dramatic twist in harassment suit against star CBS correspondent Matt Gutman See more of our coverage in your search results. Add The California Post on Google CBS News star Matt Gutman is almost in the clear after a former coworker moved to have him dropped from a harassment suit filed against the correspondent and his former network. Lawyers for ex-ABC News producer Samira Said filed a request in LA Superior Court on Friday to drop Gutman from her wrongful termination lawsuit. Former ABC News staffer Samira Said had alleged that Gutman made sexualized comments during two assignments several years ago, naming him in a lawsuit filed against the network and its parent company, The Walt Disney Co., in Los Angeles Superior Court last month. It’s unclear why the decision was made to drop Gutman from the lawsuit. Gutman’s current network, CBS News, declined to comment Saturday. The California Post contacted the correspondent for comment. CBS News boss Bari Weiss hired Gutman shortly after taking the reins in October 2025. According to the initial suit, Said claimed Gutman began discussing and rating the appearance of a female correspondent while the two were on an assignment. Other male crew members allegedly joined the conversation and tried to get Said to weigh in. She refused and told them the discussion was inappropriate, according to the lawsuit. Said also alleged a second incident occurred while she and Gutman were covering a press event for a movie release. The two disagreed about whether they should leave the work site, the suit claimed, with Gutman allegedly responding with a “sexualized insinuation” about Said in front of several coworkers. Said alleged the comments were demeaning and “reduced [her] professional judgment to a sexualized stereotype.” She is still pursuing a wrongful termination lawsuit against ABC News and The Walt Disney Co. entry.body: Alexandra Artrip, who played the youngest daughter of Sandra Bullock’s character Sally Owens in 1998’s “Practical Magic,” has weighed in on the sequel’s decision to recast her and fellow original actor Evan Rachel Wood in the upcoming sequel. Artrip played Antonia Owens alongside Wood as her older sister Kylie, but their roles were given to younger actresses Maisie Williams and Joey King, respectively, in “Practical Magic 2.” Wood spoke out about the recasting earlier in the week, saying that “no one who worked on the original movie” reached out to her. She said that she did hear from King, who took over her role as Kylie, and that she was a “sweetheart.” Artrip posted a video on Instagram and responded to comments criticizing the recastings. “I love hearing your stories and connections to the film, but I get comments like this a lot, and I see them going on a lot of content around the sequel,” Artrip said. “I think the sentiment is right, people are trying to show support for Evan and myself and the original film and everything it’s meant to so many people, but I just don’t want my stuff to be a space for negativity. Maisie and Joey are lovely actresses, and I’m sure the production team did what they thought was best for the film to be successful.” Popular on Variety She added, “I just think we should support the film, give it a shot, go in with an open mind. Nothing can take away from what the original film was, and I’m excited that we’re able to build on that world with a new novel, new content in 2026, and that it’s given me a space to revisit all those beloved memories all these years later.” “Practical Magic 2” director Susanne Bier also weighed in on the recastings, telling Variety at the premiere that it was “not personal.” “The kids in the story are right out of college, so it wasn’t really a question,” she said. “We had to recast and we had to get some kids that [had been out of college].” “Practical Magic 2” opens in theaters on Sept.

entry.title: Witkoff and Kushner meet with Putin about ending Ukraine war
entry.body: President Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin Saturday and discussed U.S. ideas for ending the war in Ukraine. Why it matters: Witkoff and Kushner want to resume direct talks between Russia and Ukraine after negotiations were suspended six months ago and the fighting has escalated ahead of winter. Witkoff and Kushner, who are expected to travel to Kyiv on Sunday, got Russia and Ukraine to agree to a short pause in airstrikes to allow the trip to take place. What they are saying: Putin told Witkoff and Kushner at the top of the three-hour meeting that he has "full trust" in the U.S. mediation between Russia and Ukraine. Witkoff thanked Putin for releasing ex-U.S. Marine Robert Gilman and for agreeing to pause airstrikes against Ukraine while U.S. negotiators are visiting Kyiv. Putin said the pause will begin at midnight Saturday Moscow time and noted that Ukraine also reduced its strikes. "We will do our utmost to provide for the safety of the negotiations," Putin said. Yes, but: Over the last several days, Russia dramatically increased its drone and missile attacks on Ukraine, including Kyiv and other major cities. The big picture: The trip to Kyiv by Trump's envoys will be the highest-level visit by a U.S. official to Ukraine since President Trump started his second term. If the U.S. government plane carrying Witkoff and Kushner touches down in Ukraine on Sunday, it will be the first international flight that lands in the country since the war started in February 2022.

entry.title: U.S. attacks 3 Iranian tankers in tit-for-tat response
entry.body: U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday after Iran fired ballistic missiles at two U.S. Navy warships, U.S. Central Command said. Why it matters: The strikes continue a tit-for-tat war that just passed the six-month mark . A U.S. official told Axios this week it had a new "tanker-for-tanker" policy approved by President Trump. Driving the news: CENTCOM said it retaliated after a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer evaded missiles fired by Iran. The U.S. attacks "permanently disabled" the M/T Downy and the M/T Stark 1, CENTCOM said in a news release. They also "completely destroyed" the M/T Kylo in the Gulf of Oman after the crew was warned to abandon ship. CENTCOM posted footage of the strikes on social media. The big picture: On the first day of the war, Trump told Axios he "can go long and take over the whole thing, or end it in two or three days." The next day, he predicted to the Daily Mail the military campaign would "take four weeks — or less." Six months later, the U.S. and Iran are still trading attacks. The latest exchange came a day after Trump called the Iran conflict "small potatoes" and two days after Vice President Vance insisted there was no war and "no active shooting" between the two. An Aug. 14–17 Economist/YouGov poll found 65% of Americans want the U.S. to make a deal to end the war as quickly as possible.

entry.title: Trump’s MAGA Inc. sends $10M to Texas in first general election spend of the year
entry.body: President Donald Trump’s super PAC is shelling out $10 million for Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign, its first general election contribution ahead of the November midterms, according to a filing made public Saturday. It’s a welcome sign for Republicans, who have implored the president to mobilize his massive campaign war chest and groused that he must be the one to pull Paxton — whom he helped to defeat popular incumbent John Cornyn in the GOP primary — over the line in Texas against state Rep. James Talarico. "High Tax Talarico wants to take money out of Texans' pockets, MAGA Inc. spokesperson Alex Pfeiffer said in a statement. "MAGA Inc. is going to ensure Texas knows about Talarico's radical policies and elects Ken Paxton to the U.S. Senate." A spokesperson for the Talarico campaign suggested the super PAC isn't telling the truth about the Democratic nominee. “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James Talarico because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system,” spokesperson JT Ennis said. Paxton's campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In an Oval Office press conference Friday, Trump pledged to pour “probably $400, 500 million” into the midterms, telling reporters the super PAC had amassed “close to a billion dollars.” The $10 million unveiled Saturday is the only amount known to have been spent by MAGA Inc. so far this general election cycle. “We’re going to spend a lot of money because we don’t want to lose our country,” Trump said. “I’m going to spend whatever amount of money necessary to try to help us, and this is money from MAGA Inc. This is my money that I control.” But with Republicans locked in hyper-competitive Senate races in a series of battleground states, and the GOP poised to perhaps lose control of the House for the first time since January 2023, the super PAC had previously refrained from spending to defeat Democrats this fall. Money from MAGA Inc. had only recently started to trickle out to boost GOP candidates, most of whom faced competitive primaries. It spent more than $827,000 to boost Sen. Darline Graham in the primary runoff in August. The super PAC raised $3 million in July and $18 million in June . Before the spend to boost Graham, MAGA Inc. hadn’t spent on a candidate since May, when it doled out $560,000 to MAGA KY , which supported Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) challenger in that month’s primary. The super PAC isn’t directly controlled by the president or the White House, and super PACs are supposed to operate independently, but candidates, including Trump, often have significant sway over the organizations. Paxton is in the middle of a closer-than-expected race against Talarico in Texas, where Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 14 points in 2024. He faces a major funding disparity and has been dogged by a wide variety of scandals that have traditional donors looking the other way.

It’s a welcome sign for Republicans, who have implored the president to mobilize his massive campaign war chest and groused that he must be the one to pull Paxton — whom he helped to defeat popular incumbent John Cornyn in the GOP primary — over the line in Texas against state Rep. James Talarico. "High Tax Talarico wants to take money out of Texans' pockets, MAGA Inc. spokesperson Alex Pfeiffer said in a statement. "MAGA Inc. is going to ensure Texas knows about Talarico's radical policies and elects Ken Paxton to the U.S. Senate." A spokesperson for the Talarico campaign suggested the super PAC isn't telling the truth about the Democratic nominee. “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James Talarico because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system,” spokesperson JT Ennis said. Paxton's campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In an Oval Office press conference Friday, Trump pledged to pour “probably $400, 500 million” into the midterms, telling reporters the super PAC had amassed “close to a billion dollars.” The $10 million unveiled Saturday is the only amount known to have been spent by MAGA Inc. so far this general election cycle. “We’re going to spend a lot of money because we don’t want to lose our country,” Trump said. “I’m going to spend whatever amount of money necessary to try to help us, and this is money from MAGA Inc. This is my money that I control.” But with Republicans locked in hyper-competitive Senate races in a series of battleground states, and the GOP poised to perhaps lose control of the House for the first time since January 2023, the super PAC had previously refrained from spending to defeat Democrats this fall. Money from MAGA Inc. had only recently started to trickle out to boost GOP candidates, most of whom faced competitive primaries. It spent more than $827,000 to boost Sen. Darline Graham in the primary runoff in August. The super PAC raised $3 million in July and $18 million in June . Before the spend to boost Graham, MAGA Inc. hadn’t spent on a candidate since May, when it doled out $560,000 to MAGA KY , which supported Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) challenger in that month’s primary. The super PAC isn’t directly controlled by the president or the White House, and super PACs are supposed to operate independently, but candidates, including Trump, often have significant sway over the organizations. Paxton is in the middle of a closer-than-expected race against Talarico in Texas, where Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 14 points in 2024. He faces a major funding disparity and has been dogged by a wide variety of scandals that have traditional donors looking the other way.

entry.title: "We're stuck:" GOP accepts Trump's all-about-me midterms
entry.body: President Trump is hitting the campaign trail and doing the last thing many Republicans want: making the 59 days to the Nov. 3 midterms a referendum on him. At the same time, they know it's inevitable. Why it matters : Most Republicans are too scared to bluntly tell Trump how unpopular he is. And Trump wants an unprecedented convention next week, ads and events to focus on him. The big picture : Their timidity aside, Republicans need Trump's low-propensity voters to turn out. So they're going along with a Trump-focused strategy that many believe could cost them credibility — along with seats in the House and Senate. "We have no choice. We're stuck on the boat with him whether we like it or not," said a top Republican campaign official who's in contact with Trump's political operation. "Now, a rising tide raises all boats," the official added. "But the only ones who sound sure about the tide rising is the White House." Driving the news: At Trump's urging, the GOP on Wednesday and Thursday is hosting an unprecedented midterm convention in Dallas, headlined by the president. Zoom in : Trump plans to speak both nights at the convention. He's also the star of his political operation's first two TV ads: The first 30-second ad, called "Toughest Guy," is all about you-know-who. The second, labeled "Tax Cut Prices," features Trump as well and would be more conventional for a campaign in which he's on the ballot. Inside the room: Trump essentially demanded the ads focus on him because midterms are referendums on a president anyway, and he wanted to tout his accomplishments, The Atlantic first reported. "I'm not on the ballot but I'm on the ballot," Trump told one confidant who relayed the conversation to Axios. "Our job is to turn Trump voters into midterm voters," a Trump adviser told Axios. The intrigue: The ads look like a de facto compromise between Trump and his political staff. "This is for the audience of one," Trump's confidant said, referring to the president. "If the boss wants it, he gets it." One Trump adviser said to expect more conventional ads: "We will be stripping the bark off of Democrats and supporting our candidates. ... It's not all Trump-focused ads." What he's saying : On Friday, Trump acknowledged to reporters that "history has said that the sitting president" sees midterm losses, but he didn't complete the thought and then talked about how "nobody's ever had a first one and a half years like we have." "We have around $1 billion that I can spend," Trump said, referring to his super PAC and political nonprofit, which together have about $800 million. "I'm allocating, probably, about $400-$500 million" for the midterms, he said. "This is my money that I control now," he said. "I can spend it for what I want to spend it for. But I'm going to help a lot of the congressmen and senators that need help." Yes, but: It's unclear how Trump could spend that much money in two months. Between the lines: Trump's message in his tax cut ads is good, Republican strategists say, but their research increasingly shows voters blame him for the war in Iran that's raising gas prices. "Diesel's at an all-time high . Gas is about $4 a gallon. We can't message that away," said another Republican who runs campaigns for a few federal candidates. Trump advisers say he'll use the bully pulpit to make his case at the convention, but his speeches tend to lack cogency and focus, and their effectiveness is questionable. "If you look at the 20 competitive House races and the six Senate races we're really focused on, this is not as dire as the media wants you to think," a Trump adviser said. "This is winnable." The backstory: Trump explained this week on the "Lt. Dan" podcast with Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick that he decided to hold the event in Dallas because "we have this big convention for the presidential election, but the midterms — people talk about it. It's very important, but there's no convention." "So ... I just came up with the idea, and we raised a lot of money." Friction point : Trump's plummeting poll numbers aside, one problem is the convention's timing: It's competing with the NFL's season-opening games, which could draw far more attention. Even Republicans' interest is limited. Many candidates aren't going . "What's the point?" yet another Republican consultant involved in federal races told Axios. "It's like what they say about a tree falling in a forest: Does it make a noise if nobody's around? Well, is it a convention if no one's really watching?" What's next: At a Rose Garden dinner Wednesday with dozens of House Republicans, Trump promised to campaign across the country in 35 races "to see if we can get everyone elected." If Trump wants to campaign for a candidate, it's going to be hard for them to say no, said one of the consultants involved in talks with MAGA Inc., the super PAC that backs Trump. "Say no to Trump, and he could punish you," the consultant said. "Say yes to him, and his presence might not help. This is the world we're in."
